beaches.label: Beaches
beaches.intro: Sandy, pebble and rocky shores — my favourite spots for a swim on the island.

items.name: Kamares
items.description: The main beach at the port — quite long and wide. Handy for a last swim before boarding the ferry home. There's a string of beach bars on one side of the beach, of which Old Captain is the most casual, old-school one with real character — you'll have a coffee, play backgammon, have a chat with the captain, and you won't pay an arm and a leg for a table or sun lounger. Next to it there are various trendier, pricier beach bars. On the opposite side of the beach is Paralia Beach Bar, usually packed — also nice, with a platform right over the water.

items.name: Glyfo (or Vlycho)
items.description: Walk through the main Faros beach and follow a little path for 3 minutes to get there. Lovely shade under the tamarisk trees — it's a beautiful spot to stay until 6–7pm, when the sun drops behind the hill and the crowd thins out. Draws a fairly young crowd. Three minutes away there's a very good bakery for coffee and snacks, plus a mini market and tavernas.
items.tips: From here a path also leads to the Chrysopigi church, about 15 minutes on foot. Along the way, the abandoned ore-loading installations of the area's old mine will catch your eye.

items.name: Fasolou
items.description: On the road to Faros there's a sign to turn left before you reach the harbour. Nice sandy beach — though there's a slightly slippery stone slab as you step into the water. A few tamarisks for shade. The vibe is mostly families, and there's a taverna too.

items.name: Platy Gialos
items.description: The most organised beach on the island, with quite a few beach bars.

nearbyLinks.name: Palmira Beach Bar
nearbyLinks.note: draws a young crowd until late afternoon/evening

items.name: Vathi
items.description: A large beach facing south-west. The nicest spot if you have your own parasol or shade is in front of the 'Elies' hotel, where there's plenty of space to spread out. There are also a few beach bars next door if you prefer a sun lounger.

items.name: Cherronisos
items.description: A small sandy beach with a jetty to dive off. Probably the most picturesque fishing village on Sifnos. On the north side of the village there are also fantastic rocks for a swim →. If you stay until sunset, climb up to Agios Georgios (15 minutes from the square — you can drive halfway) for views towards Serifos. There's a gate — open it without hesitation and go in.

nearbyLinks.name: Keramika 'I Dyskoli'
nearbyLinks.note: traditional pottery workshop, right on the beach

items.name: Fykiada
items.note: Accessible only by trail or boat
items.description: One of the cleanest beaches on the island, tucked in the south, with crystal-clear water. There's no shade at all, so bring an umbrella or a beach tent — and plenty of water, as there are no facilities on the beach. From June, small boats also run from Platy Gialos and Kamares.
items.tips: You can reach it on foot by two trails: the nearest starts from the road to Vathi (about 2 km before you reach it, a fairly flat route of ~3.2 km / 50 min), while there's also a longer route from Platy Gialos. Both are waymarked (Sifnos Trails) so you won't get lost. Trail details: sifnostrails.com.

image.credit: / Thksif2 at Greek Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons)

items.name: Chrysopigi (Saures)
items.description: A fairly small, unorganised pebble beach beside the famous Panagia Chrysopigi church. Worth it for the atmosphere of the place. It's on the right-hand side as you face the church. A dive off the Chrysopigi rocks directly opposite is non-negotiable.

items.name: Vroulidia
items.description: Not recommended. The rocks underwater are slippery and the road down has an extremely steep gradient. If you do go, leave the car at the top.

items.name: Kastro (Seralia)
items.description: A small beach below the village of Kastro. Not recommended.

items.name: Spilia
items.description: A very small, quiet pebble beach right next to the port and marina of Kamares. Ideal for a calmer swim away from the crowds of the main beach.

items.name: Gialoudia
items.description: A small cove north of Kamares, with small pebbles that gradually give way to sand and turquoise-green water. Accessible only by sea.

items.name: Tsouvales
items.description: A small secluded cove on the northern side of the island, with sand and pebbles and a lush green ravine spilling out at the back. Accessible only by sea — for example, by canoe from Cherronisos beach.

items.name: Poulati
items.description: One of my favourite rocky spots. A short dirt road leads to a small descent (5 minutes with steps). Crystal-clear turquoise water — reminiscent of Paxos.
items.tips: Swim to the left of the rock formation in the water — that's where the pebble seabed and the most vivid turquoise colour are.

items.name: Chrysopigi (rocky side)
items.note: Rocks to the right of the church
items.description: The flat rocks to the right of the Panagia Chrysopigi church (as you walk down) make for perfect sunbathing and diving spots. A must.

items.name: Kastro (Eptamartiros church)
items.description: A similar experience to Chrysopigi but with fewer people and slightly trickier rock access.

items.name: Cherronisos (rocky coast)
items.description: A charming fishing village at the northernmost tip of Sifnos. Beautiful rocky coastline, typically quiet. Park on the square and walk to the rocks.

villages.label: Villages
villages.intro: The villages of Sifnos were built inland, away from the pirates. Whitewashed, with narrow alleys and dozens of churches, each has its own character. (Draft text — refine it with your own local take.)

items.name: Apollonia
items.description: The centre of the island — this is where the heart beats. The pedestrian street 'Steno' fills with bars, restaurants and shops, and every bus passes through here. An ideal base if you want to be in the middle of the action.

image.credit: Horology at English Wikipedia (Public domain, Wikimedia Commons)

items.name: Artemonas
items.description: The most elegant village, right next to Apollonia. Neoclassical houses, captains' mansions, blooming courtyards and quiet lanes. Home to some of the island's best patisseries and bakeries.

items.name: Kastro
items.description: The old fortified settlement, built on the ancient capital and continuously inhabited for millennia. Covered passageways, Venetian coats of arms, Venetian-style balconies and the sea below. The most atmospheric place for a sunset and a stroll.

items.name: Kamares
items.description: The island's gateway — this is where the ferries dock. A beach with beach bars, tavernas, hotels and the traditional potteries. Handy for your first and last day.

items.name: Faros
items.description: A picturesque former fishing village in the south-east, with three beaches close together and a path to Chrysopigi. Calm, family-friendly atmosphere.

image.credit: Luca Conti from Senigallia, Italy (CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons)

items.name: Platy Gialos
items.description: The most organised seaside village, in the south. A large beach, hotels, tavernas and beach bars — and a base for water sports and boat trips.

items.name: Vathi
items.description: Built around an enclosed, calm bay in the south-west — until recently reached mostly by boat. Sandy shore, lake-still water and the little Taxiarchis chapel set in the sea.

items.name: Exambela
items.description: A village south of Apollonia, known for its musical tradition and for the Vrysi Monastery (17th century) with its ecclesiastical museum. Birthplace of the poet Aristomenis Provelengios.

items.name: Cherronisos
items.description: The northernmost, remote fishing village — far from everything, with fishing boats, tavernas serving fresh fish and a traditional pottery workshop. Lovely for a sunset with views of Serifos.

drinks.label: Drinks
drinks.intro: From sunset cocktails in Kastro to after-hours in Apollonia — my go-to spots for drinks on Sifnos.

items.name: Cavo Sunrise
items.description: Go for the sunset or later. Chilled-out music, generous pours and the owner Kyrios Kostas (who calls himself the Che Guevara of Sifnos) is a true character.
items.note: Not the tidiest place — but YOLO.

areas.intro: The alley (steno) of Apollonia is the heart of the nightlife. Plenty of options depending on your mood.

items.name: Botzi
items.description: Rooftop bar in the alley of Apollonia. One of the main choices for drinks with a view.

items.name: Cosi
items.description: Another rooftop in the alley, similar vibe to Botzi. These two are the main options for a more polished atmosphere.

items.name: Doloma
items.description: More alternative music and atmosphere. Located higher up in the alley.

items.name: Mantalou
items.description: Together with Doloma, the go-to spots for a more alternative crowd in the upper part of the alley.

items.name: Drakakis
items.description: A mezedopoleio (small plates bar) on the same street. A bit pricey but a great spot — and you can't get more central than this.

items.name: GRADO
items.description: The place for late-night dancing. Normally runs two floors: upstairs Greek music, downstairs international.
items.note: Ask if a reservation is needed.

areas.intro: The most beautiful village to wander through — and its scene has grown a lot in recent years.

items.name: Mosaiko
items.description: A must in Artemonas. A great mezedopoleio with a lovely atmosphere.

items.name: Diachroniko
items.description: A casual bar on the way to Mosaiko. Might catch your eye — worth a quick stop.

food.label: Food
food.intro: Sifnos is the birthplace of Nikolaos Tselementes — the father of Greek cuisine. The island has a strong culinary identity you shouldn't miss.

items.name: To Kelari
items.description: One of the best places to try authentic Sifnian cooking.

items.name: Tsikali
items.description: A taverna right on Vathi beach. Perfect for a long lunch after swimming.

items.name: Chrysopigi
items.description: A taverna right on Chrysopigi beach. Great sea views and the iconic church as backdrop.

localFood.label: Traditional Foods & Flavours
localFood.intro: The must-try foods and products of Sifnos:

items.name: Mastelo
items.description: Baby goat slow-cooked in red wine and dill inside a lidded clay pot of the same name (shaped like a casserole dish). The ultimate Sifnian recipe.

items.name: Revythada
items.description: Chickpeas soaked in rainwater and slow-cooked for many hours in a wood-fired oven with onion until they turn creamy. Traditionally the dish Sifnians eat every Sunday after church. Served with a squeeze of lemon, bread and olives (or 'egkies', as the locals call them) — pure bliss.

items.name: Revythokeftedes
items.description: Chickpea fritters — falafel before it was cool.

items.name: Kaparosalata
items.description: The island is covered in wild caper bushes hanging off stone walls. The caper salad is made with plenty of onion and some say it tastes a bit like stifado because of it.

items.name: (Xino)myzithra
items.description: A soft white cheese that is very tasty and pairs perfectly with a Greek salad, and also spread on bread. Ask for it instead of feta in a Greek salad.

items.name: Manoura
items.description: A strong aged cheese ripened in red wine, with a dark crust of wine sediment on the outside. It looks like mud on the rind — but that's where all the flavour is. Do not skip this.

items.name: Veniou Bakery
items.description: Handmade bougatsa and cheese pies in Kamares. The perfect stop right off the ferry.

items.name: Grigoris
items.description: The best traditional sweets on the island: amygdalota (almond macaroons), oven biscuits, aniseed rings and wine biscuits.

items.name: Theodorou Pastry Shop
items.description: A historic pastry shop in Artemonas, open since 1933 and now in its third generation. Famous for its amygdalota (almond macaroons) — soft and fragrant — as well as loukoumia, halvadopites, pastelia and spoon sweets.

localProducts.label: What to Take Home
localProducts.intro: Island products for gifts or for home — the taste and aroma of Sifnos.

items.name: Thyme Honey
items.description: Excellent-quality thyme honey, one of the most sought-after local products.

items.name: Capers
items.description: Fresh, dried or as leaves — harvested on the island's dry-stone terraces, they go with salads and mezes.

items.name: Cheeses
items.description: Three classic Sifnian varieties: xinomizithra, chloromanoura, and the manoura that ripens in red wine.

items.name: Almond Sweets & Traditional Treats
items.description: Amygdalota, melopita (honey pie), loukoumi, pasteli and aniseed rings — the sweets of Sifnos.

items.name: Herbs & Aromatics
items.description: Wild oregano, sage, thyme and other island herbs, gathered from the mountains.

items.name: Ceramics
items.description: Handmade clay pots and decorative pieces — the most authentic Sifnian gift. A cooking pot (tsoukali or gastra) keeps the tradition alive.

activities.label: Activities
activities.intro: From cruises and diving to hiking, climbing and cooking classes — what to do on Sifnos beyond the beaches.

items.name: Boat Tour around Sifnos
items.description: Full-day cruise around the island — secluded coves, swim stops, lunch on the boat. Morning and afternoon departures, mainly from Platy Gialos and Kamares, on traditional wooden sailboats or speedboats. If you'd rather have something more private, boat rentals with or without a skipper are also available. The best way to see Sifnos from a different angle.

items.name: Island Bus Tour
items.description: Organised coach excursions to the island's most important sights — ideal if you don't have your own wheels. Book through the local travel agencies in Apollonia or Kamares.

items.name: Horse riding
items.description: Guided rides and beginner lessons from a dedicated riding centre. The routes follow the island's old footpaths — great for those who want to see Sifnos from a different trail.

items.name: Farm visit
items.description: Two farms welcome visitors: the Narlis farm on the road to Kato Petali — cheeses, dairy products and often cooking classes (see the Workshops tab) — and Anthi Farm near Apollonia, where you milk goats, make myzithra cheese, feed the animals and enjoy a farm breakfast or dinner.

contacts.name: Sifnos Farm Narlis
contacts.note: on the road to Kato Petali

subsections.label: Sunset
subsections.intro: Two very different experiences — one easy by car, one that requires a hike.

items.name: Agios Symeon
items.description: Drive up to Agios Symeon — just 10 minutes from Kamares. Incredible views with no effort; the road goes all the way up. Popular spot — go early.

items.name: Profitis Ilias o Apsilos
items.description: The highest point on the island. ~1-hour hike from the village. Bring water and proper shoes — the reward is a panoramic 360° view.

subsections.label: Hiking
subsections.intro: Sifnos has an amazing network of some 200 km of old footpaths, with 19 waymarked routes (Sifnos Trails) — from easy strolls to full-day treks, past chapels, dovecotes, threshing floors and dry-stone walls. Maps and details at sifnostrails.com. Best in spring and autumn — in summer start early, with water and good shoes.

items.name: Agios Silivestros & the Mines
items.description: Hike in the north of the island, up to the chapel of Agios Silivestros and the old mines. Historic landscape — this is where the ancient Sifnians extracted gold and silver, which paid for the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi.

items.name: Profitis Ilias o Apsilos
items.description: Uphill hike to the highest point on the island. Best done early morning or towards sunset.

items.name: Kamares → Kastro
items.description: Traditional crossing from the port to the medieval Kastro, through the mountain villages. Stop whenever you like — it passes through all the central villages.

subsections.label: Sports & Sea
subsections.intro: For the more energetic — from the seabed to the crags.

items.name: Scuba Diving & Snorkeling
items.description: The diving centre in Kamares runs discovery dives for beginners, courses and guided dives at hand-picked spots on the island's seabed. The waters around Sifnos are clear and full of life — even a simple snorkel off the rocky shores is worth it.

items.name: Kayak, SUP & Canoe
items.description: Kayak, SUP, canoe and sea-bike rentals on the big southern beaches. On a calm morning, paddling out to the neighbouring coves is one of the loveliest ways to start the day.

items.name: Rock Climbing
items.description: Four sport-climbing crags with around 70 routes from 5b to 7b — relatively densely bolted, with anchors at the top of every route. There's no gear rental on the island: bring a 70 m rope, quickdraws and all your own equipment.

items.name: Cycling
items.description: Mountain or trekking bike rides on quiet roads and dirt tracks, on your own or with an organised excursion. Bike rentals are available on the island — but Sifnos is hilly: pace yourself.

subsections.label: Workshops
subsections.intro: Learn from the locals — cooking and pottery on the island of Tselementes and the potters.

items.name: Sifnian Cooking Classes
items.description: In the birthplace of Tselementes, learn to make revithada, chickpea fritters and other local dishes alongside locals. Classes run in Apollonia and at a local farm on the road to Kato Petali — and at the end you eat what you cooked.

contacts.name: Sifnos Farm Narlis
contacts.note: farm on the road to Kato Petali

items.name: Pottery Workshops
items.description: Try the wheel! In Artemonas the Ceramics Museum offers introductory wheel sessions for adults and clay play for kids, while in Apollonia you can paint your own piece. Many of the island's working potteries also welcome visitors — see the Culture section too.

subsections.label: Nature
subsections.intro: A large part of Sifnos is protected — ideal for quiet walks away from the crowds.

items.name: Natura 2000 Area
items.description: Since 1976 Sifnos has been designated a landscape of outstanding natural beauty. Around 2,000 hectares — from Profitis Ilias mountain to the western coast — belong to the European Natura 2000 network, with 39 bird species and 19 rare endemic species.

items.name: Flora & Fauna
items.description: Junipers (juniperus oxycedrus), mastic trees, wild olives and aromatic herbs on land; Posidonia seagrass meadows on the seabed. The centuries-old stone terraces hold the soil and tie nature and people together in harmony.

history.label: History
history.intro: A short look at Sifnos's past — from the ancient mines to the modern era.

chapters.title: Prehistoric Times
chapters.body: A centre of the Early Cycladic civilisation from the 3rd millennium BC. Tradition names Pelasgians, Carians, Leleges and Phoenicians as the first inhabitants; after the Trojan War, Ionians settled under their leader Alkenor. From the Mycenaean era survives the visitable acropolis of Agios Andreas (13th century BC).

chapters.title: Gold and Silver
chapters.body: One of the richest islands of the Cyclades: the silver mine at Agios Sostis is considered the second oldest in the world, and gold was mined at Faros and Apokofto. The Sifnians were among the first to mint gold coinage (~600 BC) and built the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi (525 BC) — the first all-marble building of mainland Greece. According to myth, when they stopped dedicating gold to Apollo, the god flooded their mines with the sea.

chapters.title: The Ancient Towers
chapters.body: More than 70 circular towers — the highest concentration in Greece — served as watchtowers and fire-signal stations, relaying messages by fire all the way to the ancient acropolises. The network was set up after the Samian raid (525 BC) and is revived by volunteers every Pentecost Sunday.

chapters.title: Byzantine & Venetian Period
chapters.body: After 1204 the island joined the Duchy of Naxos, with a Byzantine interlude from 1269. In 1307 it passed to Januli Da Corogna, who fortified Kastro on the site of the ancient capital, and in 1464 to the Gozzadini family.

chapters.title: Piracy
chapters.body: With the Aegean exposed to pirate raids, the villages were built inland. Narrow alleys, blind dead-ends and dense clustering are all defensive features — and the fires on the ancient towers warned of approaching pirates.

chapters.title: Ottoman Period
chapters.body: In 1566 the island passed to the Ottomans, keeping significant privileges and relative autonomy. In 1687 the School of the Holy Sepulchre was founded — the 'Educational Institution of the Archipelago', with 300 students — producing 3 Patriarchs and 47 Metropolitans. Seafaring and pottery flourished in parallel.

chapters.title: Modern Times
chapters.body: In the 1821 Revolution the Sifnians fought under the schoolteacher Nikolaos Chrysogelos — later the first Minister of Education of Greece. In the 19th–20th centuries the economy relied on the Tsoukalades' pottery, on shipping and on iron mining; today tourism dominates, but the traditions hold firm.

chapters.title: Names that Stood Out
chapters.body: Little Sifnos produced a disproportionate number of great names. In letters: Nikolaos Tselementes, who wrote the first modern Greek cookbook and whose name became a synonym for the genre; the poets Ioannis Gryparis (Artemonas — a major translator and first director of the National Theatre) and Aristomenis Provelengios (Exambela — MP and member of the Academy of Athens); the satirical poet and combative journalist Kleanthis Triantafyllos ('Rambagas'); and the historian Leften Stavrianos, professor at Northwestern with worldwide reach. In politics and struggle: the schoolteacher Nikolaos Chrysogelos, a 'Great Teacher of the Nation', who led the Sifnians in the 1821 Revolution and became the first Minister of Education of the modern Greek state; and Stelios Sklavainas (1907–1944), KKE deputy for Thessaloniki, one of the 200 executed by the Nazis at the Kaisariani firing range on May Day 1944.

practical.label: Practical
practical.intro: Everything practical you need for your visit to Sifnos.

items.title: Ferry
items.description: Sifnos is connected to Piraeus and Lavrio via daily routes (conventional ferries ~5 hours, high-speed ~2.5–3 hours). It also connects to Milos, Serifos, Kimolos, Folegandros and Santorini. Book tickets in advance for August — especially if you're bringing a vehicle. For the Lavrio ferry, the Magic Sea Ferries company runs a bus that takes you from the Koropi suburban railway/metro station to the boat — but you need to have selected it when booking your ticket.

items.title: Buses (KTEL)
items.description: KTEL Sifnou serves all main villages (Kamares, Apollonia, Artemonas, Kastro, Platy Gialos, Faros, Cherronisos, Vathy). Frequency is good in summer. All routes pass through Apollonia. Full timetables at sifnosbus.gr.

embed.label: 🚌 Timetables — view here
embed.note: If it doesn't load properly, open sifnosbus.gr in a new tab.

items.title: Parking
items.description: In the medieval villages (Apollonia, Artemonas, Kastro) car access is restricted. Park outside and walk in. In summer parking is tight — go early or use the bus.

items.title: Water
items.description: Tap water is NOT potable on Sifnos. Buy bottled water or ask for drinking-water fountains in the villages. Many restaurants serve filtered water.

items.title: Supermarkets
items.description: The largest supermarkets are in Apollonia and Kamares. Smaller grocers exist in almost every village. Generally open daily in summer.

items.title: Weather & Wind
items.description: When the north wind (meltemi) blows hard, move to Faros, Vathi or Platy Gialos. These beaches face South-East or South-West and stay much calmer. Always ask a local for the forecast too.

items.title: Ask the Locals
items.description: Always ask locals for tips, weather updates and any festivals or village celebrations happening during your stay. If you find a panigiri (religious feast), go — it's an experience.

culture.label: Culture
culture.intro: From summer panigyria (saint festivals) to museums and ceramic workshops — Sifnos has a living culture worth exploring.

subsections.label: Panigyria
subsections.intro: Food, wine, and dancing till dawn. The traditional saint festivals of Sifnos are some of the best in the Cyclades. Always ask locals for current times and locations — some dates shift year to year.

items.name: Agia Irini
items.description: Festival at Choni, towards Cherronisos. One of the first of the year, in spring.

items.name: Panagia Chrysopigi
items.description: The most important festival on the island. Procession of the icon followed by an open-air celebration in the churchyard.

items.name: Agios Eliseus
items.description: Festival at the chapel of Agios Eliseus (Ai Nilias). One of the first festivals of the summer.

items.name: Agios Silvestros & Gabriel
items.description: A festival in the north, at the old mines of Agios Silvestros — see the trail of the same name in the Activities tab.

items.name: Agia Marina
items.description: Festival at Agia Marina, above Kamares.

items.name: Prophet Elias of Apsilos
items.description: Festival at the highest point of Sifnos. Uphill trail, but the view and atmosphere are well worth the climb.

items.name: Prophet Elias of Troullaki
items.description: The 'other' Prophet Elias festival, on the Troullaki peak (463 m), on the same day as the Apsilos one.

items.name: Agios Panteleimon
items.description: Festival in Cherronisos, at the chapel of Agios Polykarpos. A celebration in the island's northern fishing village.

items.name: Transfiguration of the Saviour
items.description: Festival at the church of Sotira in Finikidi.

items.name: Panagia i Konchi
items.description: The festival of Panagia i Konchi, in the picturesque alleys of Artemonas. One of the big festivals of the Assumption (15 August).

items.name: Panagia Platanissa
items.description: Festival at the church of Panagia in Platanissa, the day after the Assumption.

items.name: Andreas Stratilatis
items.description: Festival at the foot of the Agios Andreas hill, below the archaeological site.

items.name: Ai Giannis of Choni
items.description: Festival at Choni, towards Cherronisos.

items.name: Agios Symeon
items.description: Festival at the small chapel of Agios Symeon with a magnificent view down to Kamares. Quieter than the August festivals.

items.name: Taxiarchis of Vathi
items.description: Festival at Taxiarchis, the picturesque little church set on the sea at Vathi.

items.name: Agios Sozon
items.description: Festival at Agios Sostis, near the island's ancient mines.

items.name: Nativity of the Virgin (Vrysiani)
items.description: The festival of Vrysi Monastery (Vrysiani) in Exambela, for the Nativity of the Theotokos.

items.name: Stavros of Choni
items.description: The Holy Cross festival at Choni, towards Cherronisos, on the eve of the Elevation.

items.name: Stavros
items.description: Local festivals at chapels dedicated to the Holy Cross. The slow closing of the Sifnos summer.

items.name: Agios Nikitas
items.description: Festival at the chapel of Agios Nikitas, in Seladi. One of the last of the season.

subsections.label: Events
subsections.intro: From food festivals to street parties — cultural events organised by local associations and friends of the island. Below are the fixed annual ones; for this season's upcoming events, see the live programme.

embed.label: 📅 Upcoming events — live programme
embed.note: Updated daily. If it doesn't load, open the events programme in a new tab.

items.name: Nikolaos Tselementes Cycladic Gastronomy Festival
items.description: Gastronomy festival honouring Nikolaos Tselementes, the Sifnian chef who wrote the first modern Greek cookbook. Workshops, seminars, and dinners by top chefs.

items.name: Radioactive Street Party
items.description: Annual street party by local radio station Radioactive. Music, drinks, and half the island out in the street.

items.name: Mousifando
items.description: Music festival organised by the Sifnos Cultural Association, featuring local and visiting artists.

subsections.label: Pottery
subsections.intro: Sifnians have long been known as 'Tsoukalades' — master potters and exporters of clay cookware. The tradition lives on in working workshops across the island. The most authentic souvenir is a clay cooking vessel (tsoukali or gastra).

items.name: Keramika 'I Dyskoli'
items.description: One of the most traditional workshops on the island, in one of its most picturesque settings — right by the sea in Cherronisos. Authentic Sifnian pottery on the wheel.

subsections.label: Museums & Sites
subsections.intro: Few but excellent — Sifnos had an important role in antiquity, with silver mines and a treasury at Delphi.

items.name: Agios Andreas Archaeological Site
items.description: Ancient acropolis from the Geometric period with sweeping views over the whole island. Important finds and a small archaeological museum on site. One of the most beautiful archaeological sites in the Cyclades.

items.name: Sifnos Folklore Museum
items.description: Collection of traditional Sifnian clothing, tools, and everyday objects. On the main square of Apollonia.

subsections.label: Churches & Monasteries
subsections.intro: Sifnos has 237 churches and monasteries — the most, relative to its size, in the Cyclades. Just a few of the most important:

items.name: Panagia Chrysopigi
items.description: The island's patron church, built on a rocky islet linked to Sifnos by a small footbridge. It guards the miraculous icon of Zoodochos Pigi, which according to tradition was found in the sea by fishermen. The rock beneath it is split in two: legend says that as pirates chased two women, the Virgin split the rock to save them. The island's biggest festival is held here on Ascension (40 days after Easter). Rocks all around for a dive.

items.name: Vrysi Monastery (Vrysiani)
items.description: The island's largest monastery, dedicated to the Nativity of the Theotokos. It houses a Museum of Ecclesiastical Art with old printed books, a gospel from 1796, sacred vessels and icons.

items.name: Seven Martyrs (Eptamartyres)
items.description: The iconic little church built on a rock in the sea, below Kastro. One of the most photographed spots on the island — perfect for a sunset and dives off the surrounding rocks.

items.name: Panagia Poulati
items.description: A blue-and-white church from 1870 on the eastern side of the island, above the rocky coast of Poulati. Wonderful views over the Aegean.

items.name: Agios Symeon
items.description: A little church on a rise above Kamares, with a panoramic 360° view over all the surrounding Cyclades. An ideal spot for sunset — and one of the easiest, since the car reaches almost to the door. Its festival is held on 1 September.

items.name: Taxiarchis of Vathi
items.description: A picturesque little church built right on the sea, at the edge of Vathi's enclosed bay. With the calm, shallow water mirroring it all around, it's one of the most photogenic spots in southern Sifnos.

items.name: Panagia i Konchi
items.description: An iconic church tucked in the beautiful alleys of Artemonas, one of the most distinctive in the village. Its big festival is held on 15 August.

items.name: Agios Georgios of Cherronisos
items.description: If you're in Cherronisos for the sunset, climb up to Agios Georgios for views towards Serifos — 15 minutes from the square (or drive halfway). Beside it stands an ancient tower, of which sadly only scattered stones survive.

items.name: Profitis Ilias Monastery
items.description: A monastery on the island's highest peak, built atop an ancient acropolis. An uphill hike but with a panoramic 360° view — see the Activities tab too.
